course.title: SQL Masterclass
course.tagline: Zero to advanced, one module at a time.
course.standard: PostgreSQL-first, with MySQL, SQLite and SQL Server notes.
course.description: Module 12 teaches COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX, GROUP BY, HAVING, NULL rules, DISTINCT aggregates, grouping sets, FILTER and aggregation performance.
outcomes: Group by one or many columns
Use ROLLUP, CUBE and GROUPING SETS

modules.title: Aggregate Functions and GROUP BY
modules.goal: Summarize rows at the right grain without inflating counts or averages.

topics.title: Introduction to Aggregates
topics.simple: Aggregate functions many rows ko ek summary value me reduce karte hain.
topics.pro: Aggregates consume a set of rows and return one value per group, turning detail rows into counts, totals, averages, minima and maxima.
points: They can run over the whole table or per group.
They ignore NULL unless told otherwise.

example.sql: SELECT COUNT(*), AVG(marks) FROM students;
example.output: One row with the row count and average.

topics.title: COUNT
topics.simple: COUNT rows ya non-null values ginata hai.
topics.pro: COUNT(*) counts rows, while COUNT(column) counts non-null values in that column.

example.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS row_count FROM students;
example.output: The number of student rows.

topics.title: SUM
topics.simple: SUM numeric values ka total deta hai.
topics.pro: SUM adds non-null numeric values and returns NULL when the input set has no non-null values.
points: Use COALESCE for a zero default.

example.sql: SELECT SUM(marks) AS total_marks FROM students;
example.output: The sum of known marks.

topics.title: AVG
topics.simple: AVG non-null values ka average deta hai.
topics.pro: AVG divides the sum by the count of non-null values, so missing values reduce the denominator rather than counting as zero.
points: NULLs are excluded from both parts.
AVG over no rows is NULL.

example.sql: SELECT AVG(marks) AS average_marks FROM students;
example.output: The average of known marks.

topics.title: MIN and MAX
topics.simple: MIN smallest aur MAX largest value deta hai.
topics.pro: MIN and MAX return the smallest and largest non-null values, using the column type’s ordering.

example.sql: SELECT MIN(marks) AS lowest, MAX(marks) AS highest FROM students;
example.output: Lowest and highest known marks.

topics.title: GROUP BY
topics.simple: GROUP BY same values wale rows ko groups me baantta hai.
topics.pro: GROUP BY partitions rows by the grouping expressions; each group produces one output row and aggregates run inside each group.
points: Every non-aggregated output column must be grouped.

example.sql: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id;
example.output: One row per course with its enrollment count.

topics.title: GROUP BY Multiple Columns
topics.simple: Multiple columns se composite groups bante hain.
topics.pro: Grouping by several columns produces one row for each distinct combination, in the order the expressions are listed.
points: Order of grouping columns does not change the groups.
More columns usually means smaller groups.

example.sql: SELECT course_id, grade, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id, grade;
example.output: One row per course-grade combination.

topics.title: HAVING
topics.simple: HAVING groups ko filter karta hai.
topics.pro: HAVING filters groups after aggregation, so it can reference aggregate results that WHERE cannot see.
points: It filters groups, not individual rows.

example.sql: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
example.output: Courses with more than one enrollment.

topics.title: HAVING vs WHERE
topics.simple: WHERE rows filter karta hai; HAVING groups filter karta hai.
topics.pro: WHERE removes rows before grouping and can use only row-level predicates; HAVING removes groups after aggregation and can use aggregate predicates.
points: Filtering early in WHERE is usually cheaper.

example.sql: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments WHERE grade IS NOT NULL GROUP BY course_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
example.output: Courses with more than one graded enrollment.

topics.title: Aggregates and NULL
topics.simple: Aggregates NULL ko ignore karte hain, COUNT(*) ko chhod kar.
topics.pro: COUNT(column), SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX skip NULL inputs; COUNT(*) counts rows regardless of NULL values.

example.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS row_count, COUNT(marks) AS known FROM students;
example.output: All rows versus rows with a known mark.

topics.title: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column)
topics.simple: COUNT(*) rows ginata hai; COUNT(column) sirf non-null values.
topics.pro: The difference matters after outer joins and with nullable columns: COUNT(*) counts the preserved row, COUNT(column) counts only real matches.

example.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS row_count, COUNT(marks) AS known_marks FROM students;
example.output: Two different counts over the same table.

topics.title: COUNT(DISTINCT ...)
topics.simple: COUNT(DISTINCT column) unique non-null values ginata hai.
topics.pro: DISTINCT inside an aggregate removes duplicate non-null values before the aggregate runs, which is useful for counting unique students, courses or days.
points: It can be more expensive than COUNT(*).

example.sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT student_id) AS unique_students FROM enrollments;
example.output: The number of distinct enrolled students.

topics.title: Grouping by Expressions
topics.simple: GROUP BY column ke bajaye expression par bhi kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: Grouping by an expression lets you aggregate by month, category or computed bucket instead of raw column values.
points: Aliases can be used in PostgreSQL GROUP BY.
The same expression should be used consistently.

example.sql: SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', enrolled_on) AS month, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY month ORDER BY month;
example.output: Enrollment counts by month.

topics.title: Aggregates with JOIN
topics.simple: Join ke baad aggregates related rows ko summarize karte hain.
topics.pro: Joining before grouping aggregates related rows, but a one-to-many join changes the grain and can inflate COUNT and SUM unless you count distinct keys or pre-aggregate.

example.sql: SELECT c.title, COUNT(e.student_id) AS enrolled FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.title;
example.output: Every course with its enrollment count, including zero.

topics.title: Aggregates without GROUP BY
topics.simple: GROUP BY ke bina aggregate poore result ko ek row me summarize karta hai.
topics.pro: Without GROUP BY, the entire input is one group, so the query returns exactly one row even when the table is empty.
points: No GROUP BY means one group.
Empty input still returns one row.

example.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS row_count, AVG(marks) AS average FROM students;
example.output: One summary row for the whole table.

topics.title: GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP and CUBE
topics.simple: Ye multiple grouping levels ek hi query me dete hain.
topics.pro: GROUPING SETS lists exact grouping combinations; ROLLUP adds subtotal levels from left to right; CUBE produces every combination.
points: GROUPING() distinguishes a real NULL from a subtotal placeholder.

example.sql: SELECT course_id, grade, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY ROLLUP (course_id, grade);
example.output: Course-grade rows plus course subtotals and a grand total.

topics.title: FILTER and Conditional Aggregates
topics.simple: FILTER se aggregate sirf matching rows par chalta hai.
topics.pro: FILTER (WHERE condition) restricts the rows an aggregate sees, enabling conditional counts and sums in one pass without CASE expressions.
points: It avoids separate queries for each condition.

example.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE marks >= 60) AS passed, COUNT(*) AS total FROM students;
example.output: Passed count and total count in one row.

topics.title: Common Aggregate Errors
topics.simple: Non-grouped columns aur WHERE me aggregates sabse common errors hain.
topics.pro: The common failures are selecting a non-grouped column, putting an aggregate in WHERE, missing GROUP BY and expecting COUNT(*) to count only matches after an outer join.
points: Group or aggregate every output column.

example.sql: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
example.output: Grouped rows with an aggregate filter.

topics.title: Performance of Aggregation
topics.simple: Aggregation memory aur indexes par depend karta hai.
topics.pro: The planner uses hash or group aggregation; filtering before grouping, indexing group keys and pre-aggregating before joins usually reduce the work.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id;
example.output: A plan with HashAggregate or GroupAggregate.

topics.title: Practical Aggregation Examples
topics.simple: Ab counts, averages aur subtotals ko real reports me combine karo.
topics.pro: A reliable aggregate report states the grain, filters rows before grouping, chooses the right count, and uses HAVING or grouping sets for subtotals.

example.sql: SELECT c.title, COUNT(e.student_id) AS enrolled, ROUND(AVG(e.grade), 2) AS average_grade FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.title ORDER BY enrolled DESC, c.title ASC;
example.output: Course report with enrollment count and average grade.

learn.q: What does an aggregate function do?
options: Reduces many rows to one value
learn.answer: Reduces many rows to one value
learn.why: Aggregates summarize a set of rows.

learn.q: What does COUNT(*) count?
learn.why: COUNT(*) counts rows regardless of NULLs.

learn.q: What does COUNT(column) count?
learn.why: NULLs are skipped.

learn.q: What does SUM ignore?
learn.why: NULL is not a number to add.

learn.q: What does AVG use as its denominator?
learn.why: AVG ignores NULLs in both sum and count.

learn.q: What does MIN return?
learn.why: MIN uses the column ordering and ignores NULL.

learn.q: What does GROUP BY do?
learn.why: Each group produces one output row.

learn.q: What must every non-aggregated SELECT column do?
learn.why: Otherwise the value is ambiguous within a group.

learn.q: Which clause filters groups?
learn.why: HAVING runs after aggregation.

learn.q: Which clause filters rows before grouping?
learn.why: WHERE runs before GROUP BY.

learn.q: Can WHERE contain an aggregate?
learn.why: Aggregates are evaluated after WHERE; use HAVING.

learn.q: What does SUM return over no non-null rows?
learn.why: There is no value to add; use COALESCE for zero.

learn.q: What does COUNT(DISTINCT column) count?
learn.why: DISTINCT removes duplicates before counting.

learn.q: What does GROUP BY ROLLUP produce?
learn.why: ROLLUP adds subtotal levels from left to right.

learn.q: What does CUBE produce?
learn.why: CUBE generates all combinations of the listed columns.

learn.q: What does GROUPING() help identify?
options: A subtotal NULL versus a real NULL
learn.answer: A subtotal NULL versus a real NULL
learn.why: It flags which columns were grouped.

learn.q: What does FILTER do in an aggregate?
learn.why: FILTER (WHERE ...) applies a condition to the aggregate input.

learn.q: What happens if you select name with COUNT(*) and no GROUP BY?
learn.why: name is not grouped or aggregated.

learn.q: Which count is zero for an empty outer-join group?
learn.why: The right key is NULL when there is no match.

learn.q: What is the main risk of aggregating after a one-to-many join?
learn.why: The joined grain repeats parent rows.

interview.q: What is an aggregate function?
interview.answer: A function that summarizes a set of rows into one value, such as COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN or MAX.

interview.q: What is the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(column)?
interview.answer: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts non-null values in that column.

interview.q: How does SUM treat NULL?
interview.answer: It ignores NULL; if there are no non-null values it returns NULL.

interview.q: How does AVG treat NULL?
interview.answer: It ignores NULL in both the sum and the denominator, averaging only known values.

interview.q: What does GROUP BY do?
interview.answer: It partitions rows into groups by the grouping expressions and produces one output row per group.

interview.q: Why must non-aggregated columns appear in GROUP BY?
interview.answer: A group can contain many rows, so the query cannot choose one value without a grouping rule.

interview.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
interview.answer: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

interview.q: Can HAVING be used without GROUP BY?
interview.answer: Yes; the whole result is treated as one group.

interview.q: What does COUNT(DISTINCT column) do?
interview.answer: Counts unique non-null values after removing duplicates.

interview.q: What is a grouping set?
interview.answer: A specified combination of grouping columns; GROUPING SETS runs several combinations in one query.

interview.q: What does ROLLUP do?
interview.answer: Produces hierarchical subtotals by grouping the listed columns from left to right, ending with a grand total.

interview.q: What does CUBE do?
interview.answer: Produces every possible grouping combination of the listed columns.

interview.q: Why does GROUPING() exist?
interview.answer: It distinguishes a NULL produced by a subtotal from a real NULL in the data.

interview.q: What does FILTER do?
interview.answer: Restricts the rows an aggregate sees, enabling conditional counts and sums in one pass.

interview.q: Why can a join inflate an aggregate?
interview.answer: A one-to-many join repeats the parent row for each child, so COUNT and SUM see more rows than the parent grain.

interview.q: How do you count matches after a LEFT JOIN?
interview.answer: Use COUNT(right_table.key), which is zero when there is no match.

interview.q: How do you return zero instead of NULL for an empty SUM?
interview.answer: Use COALESCE(SUM(column), 0).

interview.q: What is the grain of an aggregate result?
interview.answer: One row per distinct combination of grouped columns, or one row total without GROUP BY.

interview.q: How does the planner compute aggregates?
interview.answer: With HashAggregate or GroupAggregate, depending on sorting, indexes, memory and statistics.

interview.q: How can you speed up aggregation?
interview.answer: Filter early, index grouping columns, pre-aggregate before joins and avoid unnecessary COUNT(DISTINCT).

labs.title: Count rows
labs.task: Count all students.
labs.solution: SELECT COUNT(*) AS row_count FROM students;

labs.title: Count non-null
labs.task: Count all rows and known marks.
labs.solution: SELECT COUNT(*) AS row_count, COUNT(marks) AS known FROM students;

labs.title: Sum marks
labs.task: Return the total of known marks.
labs.solution: SELECT SUM(marks) AS total FROM students;

labs.title: Average marks
labs.task: Return the average known mark.
labs.solution: SELECT AVG(marks) AS average FROM students;

labs.title: Min and max
labs.task: Return the lowest and highest marks.
labs.solution: SELECT MIN(marks) AS lowest, MAX(marks) AS highest FROM students;

labs.title: Group by course
labs.task: Count enrollments per course.
labs.solution: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id;

labs.title: Multiple grouping columns
labs.task: Count enrollments per course and grade.
labs.solution: SELECT course_id, grade, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id, grade;

labs.title: HAVING filter
labs.task: Return courses with more than one enrollment.
labs.solution: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

labs.title: WHERE before HAVING
labs.task: Count only graded enrollments, then keep courses above one.
labs.solution: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments WHERE grade IS NOT NULL GROUP BY course_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

labs.title: Count distinct
labs.task: Count unique enrolled students.
labs.solution: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT student_id) AS students FROM enrollments;

labs.title: Group by expression
labs.task: Count enrollments by month.
labs.solution: SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', enrolled_on) AS month, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY month ORDER BY month;

labs.title: Left join count
labs.task: Count enrollments per course, including zero.
labs.solution: SELECT c.title, COUNT(e.student_id) AS enrolled FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.title;

labs.title: Aggregate join
labs.task: Return average grade per course title.
labs.solution: SELECT c.title, ROUND(AVG(e.grade), 2) AS average_grade FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.title;

labs.title: Aggregate without GROUP BY
labs.task: Return the total row count and average marks in one row.
labs.solution: SELECT COUNT(*) AS row_count, AVG(marks) AS average FROM students;

labs.title: ROLLUP
labs.task: Return course-grade counts with subtotals.
labs.solution: SELECT course_id, grade, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY ROLLUP (course_id, grade);

labs.title: CUBE
labs.task: Return every grouping combination of course and grade.
labs.solution: SELECT course_id, grade, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY CUBE (course_id, grade);

labs.title: GROUPING flag
labs.task: Mark subtotal rows in a ROLLUP.
labs.solution: SELECT course_id, GROUPING(course_id) AS is_total, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY ROLLUP (course_id);

labs.title: FILTER aggregate
labs.task: Count passed and total students in one row.
labs.solution: SELECT COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE marks >= 60) AS passed, COUNT(*) AS total FROM students;

labs.title: COALESCE sum
labs.task: Return zero for an empty sum.
labs.solution: SELECT COALESCE(SUM(marks), 0) AS total FROM students WHERE FALSE;

labs.title: Explain aggregation
labs.task: Explain the per-course count plan.
labs.solution: EXPLAIN SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id;

logic.q: Why does COUNT(column) differ from COUNT(*)?
logic.answer: COUNT(column) skips NULL; COUNT(*) counts every row.
There are no non-null values to add, so the result is unknown rather than zero.

logic.q: Why can AVG be misleading with NULLs?
logic.answer: It averages only known values, so the denominator is smaller than the row count.

logic.q: Why does WHERE run before GROUP BY?
logic.answer: Filtering rows first reduces the data that must be grouped and aggregated.

logic.q: Why does HAVING run after GROUP BY?
logic.answer: It needs the aggregate result for each group before it can filter groups.

logic.q: Why must every non-aggregated column be grouped?
logic.answer: A group can contain many values; without grouping the output value is undefined.

logic.q: Why can a primary key in GROUP BY allow other columns?
logic.answer: PostgreSQL recognizes functional dependency, so columns determined by the grouped key are allowed.

logic.q: Why can a one-to-many join inflate SUM?
logic.answer: The parent value repeats for each child row, so it is added once per child.
It must track unique values, often with sorting or hashing, instead of a simple counter.

logic.q: Why do grouping sets produce NULLs?
logic.answer: A column that is not part of a grouping set has no single value for the subtotal row.
It distinguishes a subtotal placeholder from a real NULL in the grouped column.

logic.q: Why is HAVING without GROUP BY legal?
logic.answer: The whole result is treated as one group, so aggregate filters can apply.

logic.q: Why is an aggregate illegal in WHERE?
logic.answer: WHERE is evaluated before grouping, when the aggregate value does not exist yet.

logic.q: Why can an index help GROUP BY?
logic.answer: An ordered index can supply grouped rows without a separate sort, enabling GroupAggregate.
It reduces the row count and prevents a one-to-many join from multiplying the values being summed.

debug.title: Non-grouped column
debug.fix: SELECT name, COUNT(*) FROM students GROUP BY name;
debug.error: column "students.name" must appear in the GROUP BY clause or be used in an aggregate function

debug.title: Aggregate in WHERE
debug.broken: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) FROM enrollments WHERE COUNT(*) > 1 GROUP BY course_id;
debug.fix: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
debug.error: aggregate functions are not allowed in WHERE

debug.title: Missing GROUP BY
debug.broken: SELECT course_id, grade, COUNT(*) FROM enrollments WHERE course_id = 10;
debug.fix: SELECT course_id, grade, COUNT(*) FROM enrollments WHERE course_id = 10 GROUP BY course_id, grade;
debug.error: a selected column must appear in GROUP BY or be aggregated
debug.expected: One row per grade in course 10.

debug.title: HAVING used for rows
debug.broken: SELECT course_id, grade FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id, grade HAVING grade IS NOT NULL;
debug.fix: SELECT course_id, grade FROM enrollments WHERE grade IS NOT NULL GROUP BY course_id, grade;
debug.error: It works, but filters after grouping instead of before

debug.title: COUNT(*) in a left join
debug.broken: SELECT c.title, COUNT(*) AS enrolled FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.title;
debug.fix: SELECT c.title, COUNT(e.student_id) AS enrolled FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.title;

debug.title: SUM of no rows
debug.broken: SELECT SUM(marks) AS total FROM students WHERE FALSE;
debug.fix: SELECT COALESCE(SUM(marks), 0) AS total FROM students WHERE FALSE;

debug.title: AVG denominator
debug.broken: SELECT AVG(COALESCE(marks, 0)) AS average FROM students;
debug.fix: SELECT AVG(marks) AS average FROM students;
debug.error: Missing marks are counted as zero, lowering the average

debug.title: Group by position
debug.broken: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) FROM enrollments GROUP BY 3;
debug.fix: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id;
debug.error: GROUP BY position 3 is not in select list

debug.title: HAVING without GROUP BY
debug.broken: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) FROM enrollments HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
debug.fix: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
debug.error: column "enrollments.course_id" must appear in the GROUP BY clause or be used in an aggregate function
